newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr ends slide with emphatic rally.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr ends slide with emphatic rally.

text.p: The Australian dollar ended two months of slide with an emphatic one cent rally Thursday as signs of economic recovery eclipsed all thoughts of a rate cut.

Figures for January showed four times more jobs created than forecast, the largest gain in 14 months. The data came hot on the heels of a mould-breaking fall in mortgage rates to 25 year lows and signs from the RBA it was in no hurry to ease again.
"It's been a great day for the Aussie and marks the first real technical sign that a bottom may have been reached," said Stephen Shuster, head of forex at Citibank Australia.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar had romped to US$0.7675/80 from an early US$0.7595/00, having already bounced offshore from Wednesday's one-year closing low of US$0.7558/63.

Crucially the currency cleared resistance at US$0.7635 where a downward sloping trendline from the December peak of US$0.8212 rested. This had capped all rally attempts, with each successive defeat reinforcing its importance as a chart barrier.

Analysts said an offshore finish above here would suggest the deep downtrend was over and bears' hopes of seeing 75 cents should be shelved for the time being. "You have to say US$0.7550 looks like a solid base now," said Shuster.
The rally had been built on the resilience of support at US$0.7550 which withstood three days of downside pressure.
It also reflected a sea change in sentiment over the direction of domestic monetary policy which began last week when unexpectedly robust wages data doused talk of a rate cut.
Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane confirmed he was in no hurry to cut rates on Tuesday, saying the economic outlook was brightening and it was logical to await fresh wage information.
The country's largest lender, CBA, did its part by slashing mortgage rates on Wednesday, leaving today's upbeat jobs data to complete the market's conversion to no-rate-cut believers.
Employment jumped 38,400, the largest monthly rise since November 1995 and far above forecats of 10,000. Unemployment stayed at 8.6 percent because more people were looking for work.

Analysts cautioned that 34,900 of the gain was in part time jobs, which paid less and were less secure than full time, but still felt it strong enough to reinforce the RBA's readiness to await the impact of the three rate cuts already delivered.

"When lagging indicators, such as employment, show signs of improvement as has been the case for the past few months, the economy is well into a renewed growth phase," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
"As a result, there would seem to be even less reason why the RBA would consider any further cash rate cuts this cycle."
The futures market feared he was right and took the March 90-day bank bill contract to 94.05, a long way from the 94.32 level held before last week's wages data.
More intriguingly the December contract had collapsed to 93.58 from a high of 93.94, implying the market was betting rates would be raised from the present 6.00 percent by year end.
Dealers said the rise in the Australian yield curve may also have gone some way to restoring Japanese interest in A$ assets as the recent weight of Tokyo selling had let up today.
Yen/A$ dual currency samurais had been all the rage with Japanese investors last year but the flow of issues dried up after the RBA cut rates for the third time in December.
That easing had narrowed the spread between Australian and U.S. bonds to levels where Japanese investors felt it no longer compensated for the greater currency risk of holding the A$.

In particular, the spread on two year bonds dwindled to less than 40 basis points, seen as a crucial threshold for Japanese interest. But all that changed this week as the gap widened out to 53 basis points, stirring speculation the Japanese may regain at least a little of their appetitte for A$ paper.
Some dealers actually detected buying interest from Tokyo in sizes not seen since December which helped boost the dollar to a 4-1/2 year high of 95.30/40 yen from 94.00/10 late here Wednesday.
The highs did not stop there as the currency shot to a five year peak on the mark at 1.2896/10 from 1.2753/65.

In the process it cleared major long term resistance stretching back to November 1991 which had previously capped rallies in 1992 and 1994. The break was considered very bullish and pointed to a significant uptrend to 1.4250 marks.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
